Senior software engineers write more code from the comfort of their homes, but they review junior employees’ work less comprehensively. Lost mentorship and undiscovered ideas can affect the future of a firm.

Such losses may be why the shift has stung new graduates in particular. A new study by Peter John Lambert of the London School of Economics and Yannick Schindler of the University of Oxford suggests remote work, not AI, is to blame for young jobseekers’ woes of late. Jobs done entirely online tend to be susceptible to being done remotely. Firms that are reluctant to let untested employees work away from their boss’s watchful eye may be choosing not to hire them at all.

So why not cancel the corporate Zoom subscription and squeeze back into the cubicle? The authors note that some employees are well-served by remote work: for example, parents and people with disabilities. For most companies a mix is best. To help bosses settle on the right number of days in-office, “In Person” features a “calculator” that asks them to add and subtract days based on the firm’s characteristics. But what executive would not say the stakes of their business are high (add two days), or that innovation is crucial to their firm’s future (add three days)? When it comes to such decisions, psychologists may be more helpful than economists.

Still, many of the book’s points are well-taken. How many days employees spend at the office may be less important than whether they overlap with key colleagues. Hot-desking is a scourge, as would-be collaborators sit together only occasionally. And if bosses want to reap the benefits of in-person culture, they also need to show face. “In Person” should contribute to an ongoing conversation about why remote work has remained so persistent if it comes with so many drawbacks. Watercooler-chat lovers, rejoice.

articles.title: Chinese tech helps repressive African governments crush dissent
articles.deck: A fascinating new book investigates the cause and effects of China’s investment in Africa

paragraphs.text: WHEN CHINA paid $200m to build a new headquarters for the African Union (AU) in Addis Ababa (pictured), it was perceived as an act of great generosity. But five years later technicians noticed something odd. Late every night the servers, which had been provided by China, whirred furiously. Data was being exported to servers in Shanghai, including confidential emails, diplomats’ memos, security-camera footage and more. Algerian and Ethiopian specialists who later swept the building reportedly found microphones hidden under desks and inside walls.

The Chinese government and the companies involved, Huawei and ZTE, all denied any wrongdoing. No surprise there. More dismaying was the public reaction of African leaders, who voiced fury not over the surveillance but towards the reporters who helped expose it. In a gripping new book, Paul Kenyon, a British journalist, argues that China is the latest external power out to gouge the continent while empowering corrupt, local power-brokers.

His broader warning is that much of Africa is being taken over by Chinese tech. Many autocratic governments are using Chinese systems to monitor their people, especially dissidents. That means snooping via mobile-phone networks installed by Chinese firms, for example. Think of the methods of information control in Xinjiang being applied in Zimbabwe, Kenya and beyond. Mr Kenyon, who has a good eye for detail but a tendency to overstate his case, alleges that Chinese engineers in Africa are the “foot soldiers of China’s digital colonialism, enabling totalitarian regimes to prosper in Africa because China wants them to”.

China’s tech is spreading rapidly across Africa thanks partly to generous loans, which make it cheap. Much of it is used to hamper free speech and browsing. A Chinese company, Geedge, exports a version of China’s Great Firewall, for example, so African governments can try to censor what citizens see online.

Nasty regimes are the keenest to learn from China. In Kampala, the hilly capital of Uganda, white poles have been erected; they are topped with some 5,000 cameras that feed images to 83 monitoring centres. This is presented to the public as a measure to cut crime: the monitors use AI, facial recognition and biometric analysis to track individuals. But it is also a tool for a repressive government: Yoweri Museveni, the president, can monitor those who support the opposition.

For years America, Britain and other rich countries have shunned contracts with Huawei and ZTE, citing security risks. No such hesitancy exists in Africa, where few governments could afford to risk damaging relations with a big trading partner. China has also provided loans for countries, including Algeria and Nigeria, to pay for satellites that it built and launched.

In a related corner of the contest for information, Mr Kenyon points to the surging number of Chinese communications staff, whom he calls “propagandists”, setting up in Africa. Xinhua, China’s official state news agency, has around 35 bureaus on the continent, more than any other news firm.

What is the end-game? China is pursuing Africa’s natural resources, including its abundant oil reserves and rare earths. But it is also trying to win political support for its challenge to Western values. China may succeed in creating a “splinternet” in Africa, with digital interaction happening only in tightly monitored spaces.

This would be a “sterile world” with no dissent, Mr Kenyon argues. It would also mark a change from today when, in order to shut up opposition voices, governments sometimes cut off millions of people from online services for months or even years. “China’s African Empire” is a clear-headed warning that, as with the AU building, China is not necessarily the benign partner it claims to be. Sometimes you need to look a gift horse in the mouth.

articles.title: Explaining the popularity of Max Richter’s compositions
articles.deck: The classical composer manages to spin even serious subjects into gold

paragraphs.text: DOES ANY musician get around as much as Max Richter? In April he will be in Las Vegas, providing musical direction for Oprah Winfrey’s “immersive symphony of senses” at the Sphere. He is on screens: his soundtrack for “Hamnet” was nominated for an Academy Award this year. And he may well be in your bedroom: “Sleep”, his eight-and-a-half-hour-long composition, has been streamed more than 2bn times.

But it is probably through “On the Nature of Daylight”, a soulful six-minute composition for string quintet from 2004, that Mr Richter (pictured) has most successfully colonised the consciousness of listeners. It heightens emotions in at least a dozen films and television programmes, including “My Brilliant Friend” and “Arrival”. It transforms millions of commutes into occasions for reverie. Listeners will hear echoes of it on “While the Flood Rages”, a new album.

Achieving such ubiquity would be a feat for any composer. That Mr Richter writes classical music makes it more remarkable. Born in Germany and brought up in Britain, Mr Richter studied at the Royal Academy of Music in London and with Luciano Berio, an Italian modernist. If you do not detect the classical pedigree in Mr Richter’s music, he may point it out to you. In an interview at his studio in the Cotswolds he relocates from the sofa to the piano to demonstrate that a falling sequence of notes from his new album is reminiscent of the music of Johann Sebastian Bach. His record label is Decca, among the most storied in classical music.

But the genre would confine Mr Richter if he did not bend it. Kraftwerk, a German electronic band, is an influence alongside American minimalists such as Philip Glass. The piano in his studio keeps company with banks of vintage synthesisers, giving it the appearance of “mission control”, he jokes. As is fashionable, he deems the conventional distinction between classical music and other sorts to be “bizarre”.

Mr Richter’s medley of influences and instincts have landed him in a musical sweet spot shared with few contemporary composers. Thanks in part to his classical chops, he collaborates with choreographers as well as film directors. “While the Flood Rages” draws from music he wrote for a ballet, “MaddAddam”, which in turn is inspired by a post-apocalyptic trilogy by Margaret Atwood, teller of “The Handmaid’s Tale”. In April the Orchestre de Paris will play the premiere of a cello concerto Mr Richter is writing.

His music has an emotional directness that gives it much wider appeal than that of most living classical composers. Mari Samuelsen, a Norwegian violinist who often performs it, finds it “extremely meditative and cleansing”, both “simple and complex at the same time”. Although film and phone are its natural habitat, Mr Richter’s music also packs concert halls. Audiences tend to be younger than at conventional classical concerts, she says, and more prone to share reactions on social media.

To some listeners the sweet spot is too sweet. Some think his partnerships with brands such as Krug champagne and Christian Dior, a fashion house, are evidence that his art lulls rather than challenges. Alex Ross, a prominent critic, has written that Mr Richter’s pieces “exude a gentle fatalism, a numbed acquiescence” even in the face of “global disaster”. Many deal explicitly with political themes. “Voices”, from 2020, incorporates text from the UN human-rights declaration. “Sleep”, Mr Richter has said, is a “protest” against a “very super-industrialised, intense, mechanised way of living”. “Daylight” comes from an album that opposes America’s war in Iraq. Yet most of the time the strife seems to be happening in the distance.

“While the Flood Rages” considers the aftermath of apocalypse, environmental vandalism and corporate greed. Mr Richter says the music is “more highly coloured” than what he normally composes, echoing the “stylistic omnivorousness” of Ms Atwood’s writing. Synthetic and recorded sounds—of water, of gunfire—suggest a world made strange and threatening. But Mr Richter’s sensibility has the last word. Piano, strings and a church-like choir, sometimes in counterpoint with eerier music, seem to suggest that something good will prevail. The listener, unsettled at first by the album’s dystopian theme, may come away consoled.

That is often the effect of Mr Richter’s music. Rather than depict evil, he imagines alternatives to it. “We’re flooded with negativity, with negative images and negative storytelling,” largely because of social media, he says. “I’m looking to celebrate and elevate the things that are not that, which are ordinary…human qualities which have been with us for ever and will continue to be with us, but are easy to overlook.” While floods rage, Mr Richter offers audiences a life raft. No wonder he’s so in demand.
Correction (November 5th 2026): An earlier version of this story said that “On the Nature of Daylight” could be heard in “Black Mirror”. That was incorrect. Sorry.

articles.title: Economic data, commodities and markets
Dolores Huerta fought for farm-workers’ rights—and kept devastating secrets
articles.deck: The labour activist died on October 28th, aged 96

paragraphs.text: IN LATE November 1986 the United Farm Workers of America (UFW), a labour union, was ready to celebrate. Earlier that month, then-president Ronald Reagan signed into law the Immigration Reform and Control Act, for which the UFW had spent months lobbying. It offered undocumented immigrants long resident in America a path to citizenship, and gave farm workers who could prove 90 days of employment legal permanent residency. It also penalised employers who knowingly hired undocumented workers, whom the union feared would drive down wages and serve as scabs during a strike.

Shortly before a news conference to mark the legislative win, one of the UFW’s founders, César Chávez, told another founder, Dolores Huerta, that she was needed in Florida. A crisis, he said. So of course, she went, because that’s what she did: go where workers needed her. But when she got to Florida, she found there was no crisis. Nobody was expecting her. “They just wanted to get me out of the way so they could take credit for the work,” she said later. “Straight male-chauvinist trick.”

But hardly uncommon, as one fellow activist recalled: “The assumption was that [Chávez] was the leader, and Dolores was the housekeeper of the movement.” In fact, they founded the union together—though unlike him, she had to balance work with raising her 14 children. With his soulful dark eyes, conversational speaking style and love of the microphone, he was the charismatic front man. But she was the union’s chief negotiator. He could make the speeches; there were also boycotts to organise, contracts to negotiate and people who needed help.

Her mother, Alicia, had a similar streak of dogged practicality. After a divorce, Alicia took her three children from New Mexico to Stockton, California, in the Central Valley, California’s agricultural heartland. After stints as a waitress, cannery worker and restaurateur, Alicia ran a 70-room hotel that welcomed migrant workers, often waiving room fees if they were too steep. Alicia, Dolores recalled, “thought she was their mother”, and gave them curfews, made sure they sent money home and didn’t drink away their paychecks, and invited them to dances so they could meet nice girls and settle down—which many did.

From Alicia, who participated in a cannery-workers’ strike in 1938 and joined civic groups in Stockton, Dolores learned about activism, which was nothing more than helping people who needed help, and speaking up for people who could not advocate for themselves. After training as a teacher, she turned to full-time organising in her 20s, when she joined the Community Service Organisation in Stockton. Its founder introduced her to Chávez, and soon afterward the two founded the group that would, after merging with another farm-workers’ group, become the UFW.

From the start, she held her own. As an “experienced lobbyist”, she wrote to Chávez, “I am able to speak on a man-to-man basis with other lobbyists.” Elected officials learned to fear her. She was “indefatigable” and “unorthodox”, recalled one state senator from California. “Dolores will bring in hundreds of people, and they’ll camp outside your office.”

And although sleeping in a Senate hallway sounds uncomfortable, it was nothing compared with what her union members were used to. They worked in the fields for 16 hours a day. There were no toilets: female workers had to squat behind a towel or a blanket. The only drinking water sat baking in a tank under the sun all day. No health care or unemployment insurance, no recourse if the farm owners cheated them.

So she and Chávez got to work. In 1965 their union, which mainly represented Mexican farm workers, joined 2,000 Filipinos on strike at vineyards near Delano, California. Growers hired scabs and refused negotiations, figuring they could force the workers to back down, as they had before.

But times were changing. Strikers drew support from civil-rights activists including Robert F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King junior. They borrowed tactics from the civil-rights movement, calling for boycotts of table grapes. By 1970 the growers had given in, agreeing to raise wages and recognise the union. Membership in the UFW swelled, and five years later California passed a law protecting farm-workers’ rights to unionise, and making migrant workers eligible for health insurance and other benefits.

Chávez became a hero, giving his name to streets, parks and schools across California and beyond, despite whispers about his authoritarian tendencies, his insistence on personal loyalty and subservience. She kept doing the work, campaigning for women’s rights and encouraging them to run for office, picketing and protesting. Age barely slowed her; a policeman broke her ribs and ruptured her spleen during a demonstration when she was almost 60.

But not until this year did Dolores reveal her deepest secret: Chávez, who died in 1993, had raped her in 1966. He had pressed her into sex years earlier. Two of her children were his. She never spoke up because “I didn’t want to hurt the movement.”

A New York Times investigation found that he assaulted and molested multiple women and girls, some as young as 12. Sexism pervaded his union. Liz Sullivan, a UFW organiser who was raped by two men after an organising meeting, recalled that union members berated her and female colleagues who spoke out about the treatment of women. The male executives had no patience for “women’s lib and all that other bullshit”.

In recent months, statues of Chávez have come down and parks renamed. Some blamed Dolores, too, for keeping quiet and dismissing their complaints about being sexually harassed and assaulted by their colleagues. Ms Sullivan took a more charitable view. She urged people to “see her as a human being, in all her beauty and with all her faults, just like the rest of us”.

articles.title: Politics

paragraphs.text: Curfews were imposed in Paris, Lyon and other cities following the worst rioting and looting in France in years. More than 2,000 people were arrested as masked casseurs, or hooligans, targeted shops, businesses and political premises. The roof of the town hall in Limoges, which withstood two world wars, collapsed after it was set on fire. The government admitted the police had lost control of the protests. The French president addressed the nation and said “nothing justifies” the violence. Marine Le Pen, the right-wing front-runner in next year’s presidential election, warned of a threat to democracy and blamed Mr Macron and the left. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the left-wing’s candidate, denied he was stirring up trouble by urging support for the protests.

Widespread looting accompanied similar protests in Italy. The government announced new security steps that allow the police to detain under-18s for 12 hours, among other measures. To prevent further unrest hundreds of soldiers were deployed to Milan, which has borne the brunt of the trouble and saw luxury-goods shops ransacked.

In Albania student-led protests over corruption, poor education and a lack of jobs spread from Tirana to other cities and towns. Riot police used tear-gas and rubber bullets against the demonstrators when they reached the Ministry of Education. Edi Rama said he would not resign as prime minister, and warned that the protesters were endangering Albania’s path to membership of the EU.

Volodymyr Zelensky flew to Oslo for a meeting with Steve Witkoff, Donald Trump’s envoy, amid a deterioration in relations between Ukraine and the White House. Earlier, Mr Trump took another step towards favouring Russia by waiving sanctions mandated by the Graham Act, which he signed into law last month. Mr Zelensky criticised Mr Trump’s waiver, arguing that the act was “supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia”. The Americans described the meeting in Oslo as constructive. Mr Witkoff then flew to St Petersburg for talks with Vladimir Putin. The Kremlin said Mr Putin had agreed to restart three-way peace talks.

At his meeting with Mr Witkoff Mr Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American citizen, had been released from prison. Mr Hubbard, 74, was arrested in 2022. The Russians claim he was manning a checkpoint in Ukraine; his family have rejected accusations that he is a mercenary. His release is another indication of Mr Trump’s closer relations with Moscow. The president had personally called on Mr Putin to set Mr Hubbard free.

Britain said it would deploy fighter jets and a transport aircraft to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom against attacks by the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran. The jets will help protect infrastructure and residential areas, but will not conduct offensive strikes against the rebels. In Yemen the Houthis fired missiles at a training camp for government forces, killing at least 73 people. The Yemeni government is allied with the Saudis.

Egypt’s president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sisi, also pledged to help the Saudis, and asked parliament to approve the deployment of combat forces. The extent of any Egyptian involvement in the conflict is unclear. Turkey’s parliament was also considering a plan to send military personnel to Saudi Arabia.

More than 80 people were killed in a drone strike near a market in southern Sudan, most of them commuters on their way home from work. The Rapid Support Forces, which controls the area, blamed the strike on the army, which it is fighting in a civil war. Another drone hit a town in a disputed region near the border with South Sudan, killing at least 150 people. Such attacks causing mass civilian casualties have become increasingly common in the three-year conflict.

A former Rwandan soldier and vocal critic of Paul Kagame, Rwanda’s president, was found beheaded near Kampala, the capital of neighbouring Uganda. Robert Kabera, who fled to Uganda in 2020, had recently posted on social media that he feared for his life. He is not the first exiled Rwandan dissident to turn up dead in gruesome circumstances.

Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola since the Democratic Republic of Congo announced an outbreak of the disease in May. Authorities said the patient had travelled to Nigeria from Uganda. The Ugandan government said there were currently no active cases of the disease in the country.

America’s State Department reported that 300,000 visas have now been revoked during Donald Trump’s second term, up from the 175,000 that had been tallied up to early August. Announcing the new numbers an official reiterated the administration’s policy: “zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law”.

A non-binding referendum in Alberta saw more than 75% of voters back an option to remain a province of Canada, rather than start the process of holding a binding referendum on splitting away. Mark Carney hailed the outcome as a victory for “unity”. “Canada is so much greater than the sum of its parts,” he said. However, Albertans did back other measures in the referendum to give the province more control over immigration.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro debated each other ahead of Brazil’s presidential election run-off on October 25th. Polls show the race has narrowed since the first round on October 4th, when Mr Bolsonaro took 47% of the vote to Lula’s 45%.

Marco Rubio, America’s secretary of state, met Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, India’s foreign minister, in Mumbai for talks on finalising a trade deal. The pact has been held up for months because of tensions over American tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. But Mr Rubio now says an agreement is “very, very close”.

More than 9,500 police officers were deployed in Jakarta to deter student-led protests that were called to mark the second anniversary of Prabowo Subianto’s inauguration as Indonesia’s president. The deterrence worked, as few students gathered to demand Mr Prabowo do more to tackle the cost of living and other grievances. The president’s approval rating has plunged since taking office. MSCI, a global index service, warned that it might remove Indonesia’s emerging-market status because of its “market dysfunction”. Downgrading Indonesia would force many tracking funds to sell their Indonesian assets.

Japan’s space agency launched a spacecraft on a five-year mission to collect samples from Phobos, one of two small moons that orbit Mars, the first-ever return journey from the planet’s system. The spacecraft will enter Martian space in August 2027, landing on Phobos at some point in the following years. A rover will use a robotic arm to collect moondust. If all goes well, the spacecraft will depart in 2030 and return to Earth in 2031.

articles.title: Business

paragraphs.text: Elon Musk floated the possibility of merging SpaceX and Tesla. There is a “lot of merit” in combining the companies, he said, and the boards of both have created independent committees to explore their options (as the boss and largest shareholder in both firms Mr Musk is not on the committees). A merger would bring together Mr Musk’s AI ambitions for data centres, driverless cars and robots. SpaceX, meanwhile, reported quarterly revenue of $14.6bn, up by 161% year on year, $7.6bn of which came from AI (which it calls SI, or super intelligence). Mr Musk has pledged to give every child in America one SpaceX share, currently worth nearly $160, next year.

Tesla earlier demonstrated its new Roadster sports car; the demonstration vehicle was modified with SpaceX-derived thrusters and able to flip mid-air and land safely again. The electric-carmaker reported a surprise positive cashflow in its latest earnings.

Market jitters resurfaced about the huge investments being made in AI. CoreWeave, which rents out data-centre capacity, saw its bonds and share price plunge amid worries that it will not be able to service its debt. The sell-off spread to other “neocloud” companies. Meanwhile, the share price of Elice, an AI-infrastructure company, fell by 32% on its first day of trading in South Korea.

Anthropic registered a net loss of more than $80bn in the first half of this year, according to press reports, mostly because of an accounting charge related to bonds that could be eventually converted to shares. The frontier-AI firm is expected to make its stock-market debut in mid-November. Anthropic is to hand over 5% of its shares to a new public-benefit fund it has created to work in AI safety and examine AI’s impact on the jobs market, among other things.

Meta’s third-quarter revenue grew by 26%, year on year, to $64.6bn. The company rolled out its Muse personal AI agent in September. Meanwhile, a court in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn to the state after it was found to have misled users about privacy.
Barclays, a big British bank, revealed that it is cutting 5,000 jobs this year because of efficiencies from adopting AI. Most of the jobs will be among developers and other support services.

Stock in Netflix slid again after the streaming giant reported its slowest sales growth in three years. Revenue grew by 11.8% in the third quarter, year on year, to $12.9bn. It expects even lower growth of 11.5% in the fourth quarter. Media reports of the company’s woes as it struggles with slowing subscriptions read like a Hollywood movie plot, with both the head of film and the head of content summarily dismissed from their positions and the announcement of 1,000 job cuts. Despite massively increasing its spending on content, Netflix is no longer producing a string of hits.
GDP expanded in China by 4.5% during the third quarter, year on year, an improvement on the 4.3% recorded in the second quarter. China’s exports boom is offsetting weak domestic demand.

The riots in France helped push the yield on French ten-year government bonds above 5% for the first time since 2002, as investors bet that budgetary reforms would be delayed. Carrefour, a big supermarket chain, cut its annual profit forecast and blamed the violence, which it thinks will deter shoppers. Insurance losses from the weekend’s unrest are expected to reach €1bn ($1.1bn), exceeding the €700m in losses incurred over a week of rioting in 2023.

The developers of the PHP programming language issued a fix that they urged users to download immediately, after an OpenAI-led consortium discovered two critical vulnerabilities. PHP shores up a large part of the internet, running in the background of websites, hosting platforms and control panels. Some governments, including in Finland and the Netherlands, took some websites offline while they worked on the issue. America’s National Security Agency recommended that systems be taken offline if users couldn’t apply the mitigations. The fix will have alerted criminals to the vulnerability of servers.
Britain’s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September. Markets are now all but certain that the Bank of England will raise interest rates at its meeting in November.

The British government at last approved the development of the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, the first big endorsement of a fossil-fuel project under Andy Burnham as prime minister. The governing Labour Party has pledged to deliver a net-zero carbon emissions policy. Greens are furious, but Mr Burnham said it would protect jobs. Unions hailed the decision. The government is now under pressure to approve the Rosebank oil project, which environmentalists also vehemently oppose.

UniCredit, Italy’s second-largest bank, won approval from the European Central Bank to take over Commerzbank, a big German lender. Having secured 48% of Commerzbank’s shares, UniCredit thinks it will take control of the bank by the end of the year.

The IPO of Jio Platforms, Mukesh Ambani’s telecoms firm, was fully subscribed just two hours after it opened. The flotation is expected to raise $3.2bn, making it India’s biggest-ever listing. The shares start trading on October 28th.
