Science advocacy groups “have this extreme fixation on budgets”, he says. “Academia just needs to get out of this zero-sum mindset.”

But separately from such squabbling, many private science experiments have already begun. One of the most notable of these is Convergent Research, a Massachusetts-based nonprofit founded in 2021 to fund “focused research organisations” (FROs). Its grantees often want to create a specific tool rather than answer a purely academic question, say co-founders Anastasia Gamick and Adam Marblestone. Convergent gives researchers $20m-50m and between three and seven years to carry out their project. Afterwards, its staff will help them decide what to do with the results. One FRO creates sets of tools that labs and companies can use to study non-model organisms. Another produces an interface that uses ultrasound waves to read brain activity.

Another entrant to the world of private science is Episteme, a company launched in 2025 by Sam Altman of OpenAI and Louis Andre, then a little-known researcher. Rather than demanding pre-set targets or papers, Episteme hopes to give its lead researchers near-total freedom. While the select few it funds often have an approach in mind to solving their chosen problem, Episteme offers them the flexibility to adapt. “If an idea fails, which in science is something that happens very often, you should be able to pivot and try a different angle,” says Mr Andre.

The approach is an appealing one. Charles Marcus, a physicist, says he left a tenured position at the University of Washington to work at Episteme because he felt it would enable him to work across disciplines without needing approval from staid bureaucrats. “We’re not building academic departments in which nobody talks to each other,” he says. Nor will he and other lab leads need to apply for grants or wait for months to hire junior researchers. And while publishing papers is encouraged, it is not mandated. The main constraint on their work is that it should represent a commercial opportunity.

Many important questions fall outside that scope and will have to remain within universities. And besides, not every attempt at private science has flourished. Arena BioWorks, a private biomedical institute founded in 2023, shut down after less than two years. But whereas Arena’s funders reportedly expected quick payouts, Mr Andre says his backers, who have funded Episteme from their personal fortunes, are committed for the long haul. And Episteme, unlike Arena, is not betting on one specific area of research, either. “If a programme fails, it’s okay. We can recycle it and repurpose the resources into something else,” he reckons.

Between federal support, independent experiments and a coming wave of AI-fuelled cash, private-science initiatives are “seeing the stars align,” says Mr Marble-stone. Historians of science and technology argue the post-war system cemented American hegemony. In the bet on private science the stakes are high, both for boffins and for America.

articles.title: Japan’s mission to Mars’s moons takes off
articles.deck: It will collect samples and search for signs of ancient life

paragraphs.text: ORBITERS, LANDERS and rovers have travelled to Mars, but none has returned. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) intends for that to change. On October 20th its Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission lifted off from Tanegashima, an island in southern Japan. The probe will spend the next year travelling to Mars, where it aims to land on Phobos, the larger of the planet’s two moons, collect at least ten grams of rock and dust, and return the haul to Earth in 2031. Planetary scientists hope the mission will resolve a long-standing puzzle: how Mars’s moons were formed—and, in the process, reveal much about the planet itself.

Phobos and Mars’s other moon, Deimos, are small, respectively about 22km and 12km across, and look like lumpy potatoes. That might suggest they are asteroids that were captured by Mars’s gravitational field after straying too close. Captured asteroids, however, usually have tilted, elliptical orbits, whereas both moons follow nearly circular paths around the planet’s equator. That hints at another possible origin: a giant collision that threw debris into orbit that later gathered into moons.

JAXA has spent over a decade developing MMX, working with the space agencies of America, Europe and Australia. The mission builds on Japan’s record of returning samples from space. Its Hayabusa mission collected small amounts of grains from Itokawa, an asteroid which comes close to Earth, and brought them home in 2010. Its successor, Hayabusa2, brought back five grams of material—well above the mission’s target—from Ryugu, another near-Earth asteroid, in 2020. The samples proved rich in water-bearing molecules and organic compounds, offering clues to how asteroids may have carried the ingredients for life to Earth.

MMX’s mission is more demanding. Phobos’s surface gravity is roughly one-2,000th of Earth’s, but it is 40 times greater than Ryugu’s. That is strong enough to pose a crash risk for a delicate spacecraft, explains Erik Asphaug, a planetary scientist at the University of Arizona. The Hayabusa missions also followed a “touch-and-go” method in which the spacecraft briefly kissed the asteroids. In contrast, MMX will land on Phobos and extract samples from beneath its surface.

And MMX’s makers want to do a lot more during its three years orbiting Mars. An instrument called MEGANE (pronounced “meh-gah-neh”, like the Japanese word for spectacles), developed by NASA, will measure gamma rays and neutrons given off when cosmic rays hit Phobos, thus revealing its chemistry. A small European rover will explore its surface. After departing Phobos, MMX will conduct fly-bys of Deimos to observe it, too, up close.

If the samples make it safely back to Earth, scientists reckon they might settle which of the two origin stories is true. If Phobos is a captured asteroid, its rocks may resemble meteorites from elsewhere in the solar system. If it instead formed after a giant impact, it will contain melt fragments generated by intense heating.

Whatever Phobos’s history, its proximity to Mars means it should also have collected material blasted off the planet by asteroid impacts. Martian debris should make up about 0.1% of the samples MMX collects. Scientists already have Martian meteorites, but these are mostly hard volcanic rocks that survived the journey through space and Earth’s atmosphere. Sara Russell, a planetary scientist at the Natural History Museum in London who will help analyse MMX’s samples, hopes the mission could recover softer sedimentary material. “That’s the material where we might see biosignatures,” she says, offering clues to whether Mars was once habitable.

There is reason to wonder. Ancient riverbeds and lake deposits suggest Mars once had liquid water and a thicker atmosphere. Unlike the planet itself, its moons have undergone little geological change. They may therefore have preserved fragments of that distant past like a time capsule, says Elizabeth Tasker, an astrophysicist at JAXA. The two small moons could thus help answer a much bigger question: whether life existed on the red planet.

articles.title: The second may soon be redefined
articles.deck: Several atomic clocks are competing for the job

paragraphs.text: IT TAKES ABOUT a second to say “caesium atoms”. And, for nearly 60 years, caesium atoms have said how long a second lasts. That is because caesium-133, an isotope of caesium, switches between two energy states when exposed to microwave radiation, at a rate so regular you could set your watch by it. Indeed, atomic clocks use this steady rhythm to measure time. According to the International System of Units, a second is 9,192,631,770 cycles.

But not for much longer. On October 13th the world’s top metrologists convened in Versailles for the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), as they have done roughly once every four years since 1889, to discuss the science of measurement. After three days of debate, they set themselves a deadline: by 2030 they will decide how to redefine the second.

The CGPM oversees the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), which sets the global standard for the passage of time. It does so by combining measurements from hundreds of atomic clocks based in laboratories around the world, to account for small fluctuations which can cause errors in each individual reading. The result is a single standardised time that co-ordinates everything from financial transactions to satellite navigation.

But the BIPM has a problem. To check the accuracy of its standardised time it uses a set of newer clocks, based on different chemical elements, which can measure time more precisely than the best caesium clocks can. Checking the accuracy of the newer clocks requires a definition of the second itself. Using that from a caesium clock is like trying to measure the width of a hair using a ruler whose divisions are wider than the hair. To run the clockwork like clockwork the CGPM needs to untie the second from caesium.

Kyle Arnold, a physicist at the National University of Singapore, is part of a team developing a clock based on lutetium ions. While caesium clocks use microwave radiation to trigger transitions between the atom’s energy states, Dr Arnold’s device uses lasers. Such optical clocks “tick” more quickly, allowing time to be measured more finely. Writing in Nature, in September, Dr Arnold’s group reported its lutetium clock had a tick about 1,000 times more regular than the best caesium devices.

Atomic clocks must work reliably in different places around the world. Dr Arnold’s device, however, is the size of a room and yet to leave his Singapore lab. Other, more portable, contenders include optical clocks based on ytterbium and strontium atoms suspended by lasers. These come with their own issues. A study published in Physical Review Letters, in July, found that measurements comparing optical clocks based on these elements disagreed with earlier results by more than their known uncertainties could explain.

Metrologists must now decide which atomic transition is promoted to the official standard. That requires consensus among yet another team of time lords: the Consultative Committee for Time and Frequency, who are advising the BIPM and CGPM on the second’s fate. With the deadline set for 2030, they have about 100m seconds to reach an agreement.

articles.title: Is the internet still safe?
articles.deck: A string of cyber-security incidents has caused websites to go dark

paragraphs.text: PITY THE cyber-defenders. Occasionally, the industry must burst into action following the unheralded revelation of a vulnerability in some widely used software. Rarely, however, must they do so several times in the same week.

On October 20th the security teams at major web browsers received an unusual email. It read “we have a problem here” and was accompanied by a file containing eight private security keys: randomly generated numbers used to encrypt communications across the entire internet. Such keys should be 116 digits long to ensure security. Those in the email, originally issued by an Indian authority, were no longer than three. One was a private key of just “4”. To top things off, the email was signed simply “Wayne”.

Revoking such keys from important central databases is manageable. Checking every system has updated accordingly is hard work. Major web browsers keep their blacklists up-to-date, but many internet-connected systems do not adjust so easily. Some, like many Linux systems, require an active software update; others, like some command-line tools on MacOS, must be manually fixed.

Defenders were busily plugging those gaps when, on the morning of October 21st, another problem arrived. A pair of vulnerabilities had been exposed in PHP, a venerable programming language which underpins tens of millions of web applications, including message boards, financial portals and government websites. A patch was promised for the same afternoon. In the meantime, affected organisations were advised by governments to take their systems offline entirely—an instruction not issued lightly. Several government websites in Europe went dark.

The advice proved to have been reasonable. Hours after news of the vulnerability broke, and with over 12 hours before a patch was due, its details leaked. The vulnerability was as bad as it gets: a recipe for unauthorised remote code execution (RCE), letting an attacker take control of machines running PHP. Exploiting the vulnerability, as demonstrated by at least one widely shared proof-of-concept, was simple.

There is no direct link between the two weaknesses, but one strong relationship: both vulnerabilities seem to have been discovered by AI. The PHP vulnerability was found independently by two members of an AI cyber-defence consortium led by OpenAI, an American firm. The dodgy security keys were “possibly” found using AI too, according to eMudhra, the Indian company which issued them. Certainly, the method of disclosure suggests an unusual approach to research.

By October 22nd two further vulnerabilities had been published. GitLab, a software development tool, announced a patch for a weakness affecting 12 years of releases that could allow its own RCE, ranking it ten on a ten-point severity scale. Oracle, a tech giant, fixed a similar weakness in Java, its widely used programming language, and ranked the severity 9.1. AI was probably used to uncover these flaws, too.

The episodes illustrate an uncomfortable reality of AI-powered cyber-security: fixing an issue sets a timer for its exploitation. The PHP bug was announced with 18 hours notice before a patch was released, in an effort to prepare defenders to install the update with alacrity. But an accidental release of a video demonstrating the vulnerability allowed others, ai in hand, to reverse-engineer the problem and work out how to exploit it. Shortly after, a security company published its version of the fix six hours early, allowing any attacker to examine exactly what was fixed, and therefore uncover more details of the weakness in unpatched systems.

Defenders once faced the difficult problem of finding the flaws in their own software before attackers did. Now they have a different challenge: with AI exposing a plethora of weaknesses, how can they spread news of the fixes to their users, without tipping off their enemies in the process?

articles.title: Can joggers outrun injury?
articles.deck: Patience when training goes the extra mile

paragraphs.text: KNEE PAIN in joggers is prevalent enough to be a term of art. “Runner’s knee”, an ache around the kneecap, was among the most common complaints in a study of 3,669 runners published in the Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine (OJSM) in 2021. But it is only one of an assortment of “overuse” injuries: those caused by training that, though tolerable in parts, cumulatively exceed the body’s capacity to recover.

Such problems can compound. The study found that a previous injury increased the odds of another by 62%. Hence a widespread worry that a lifetime of running will wear down joints and eventually lead to arthritis. How can runners keep injuries at bay?

Throwing money at the problem does not help. A review published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, in 2022, found little evidence that different running-shoe designs affect their owners’ susceptibility to injury. The OJSM study from 2021 concluded that stretching before a jog did not help, either.

Instead, when taking up running or increasing the distance covered, the old adage of “slow and steady” is the one to follow. Novices report injuries more than twice as often as experienced runners, according to a review published in Sports Medicine in 2015. Some of this may be down to differences in expectations, says Rasmus Nielsen, an epidemiologist at Aarhus University in Denmark. A beginner might panic and report a twinge that a more experienced runner knows will pass on its own.

But doing too much too soon is a risk even for seasoned sprinters. A study of 5,205 runners published by Dr Nielsen and his colleagues in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, in 2025, found that running 10-30% farther in a single session than the previous month’s longest run was associated with a 64% higher rate of overuse injury.

Increasing training load slowly gives the body a chance to adapt. Using tendons stimulates collagen production, causing them to stiffen and thicken so that they are more resilient to strain. Repeated impact activates bone-strengthening cells known as osteoblasts, gradually increasing resilience to stress fractures. And, rather than damaging knee cartilage, running strengthens the muscles that help protect the joint.

Building resilience takes time. Changes in tendons occurred in studies lasting around 8 to 12 weeks, according to a review published in Sports Medicine in 2015. Increases in shinbone density have been detected after eight weeks of intensive military training. Another study found that bone mineral density improved after six months of resistance and jumping training.

To be on the safe side, Dr Nielsen recommends keeping any single run to no more than 5% longer than the past month’s longest run, and that any week’s total not exceed 110% of the previous week’s. For beginners, particularly those with high body-mass indices or a history of injury, 3km of cumulative walking and running in the first week of training is a safe starting point.

Happily, there is little evidence that running is associated with long-term joint problems. A study of 3,804 marathon runners published in Sports Health, in 2024, found no association between running history and the risk of arthritis. Accidents involving the knee, such as tears in its cartilage, can cause persistent issues. But as Dr Nielsen points out, such injuries can strike anyone. With sufficient caution, joggers can keep going for the long run.
After a free, evidence-based guide to health and wellness? Sign up to our weekly Well Informed newsletter.

articles.title: Are film critics as snooty and out of touch as people think?

paragraphs.text: Whether a film is good enough to warrant a trek to the cinema is not always easy to ascertain. Recently viewers have praised “Digger”, a satirical black comedy about a wealthy oil tycoon whose company triggers an environmental catastrophe. It has a 76% audience-approval score on Rotten Tomatoes, a review aggregator. But critics did not dig the film: only 53% reviewed it positively, complaining it was ponderous and preachy. Fans calling themselves “Digger Nation” have mobilised online to defend the movie.

Signals about films’ quality can be confusing to decipher. In April fans judged a biopic of Michael Jackson to be a thriller, with 97% of them enjoying it. But most critics thought “Michael” was bad. In January “Melania”, a documentary about America’s First Lady, reflected the politically polarised times, with a 90-point gap. “An absolute masterpiece!” gushed one audience member. “Gilded trash”, said the Guardian.

Critics and audiences have often failed to see eye to eye. The history of film criticism is littered with judgments that aged badly. (Pity the reviewer who dismissed “Citizen Kane”, now considered one of the greatest films ever made, as “well-intentioned, muddled, amateurish”.) Today many think that critics seem out of step—perhaps more than ever before.

But are they really? To test whether critical and popular opinion are drifting apart, The Economist compiled two decades of reviews of more than 10,000 films from Metacritic, an aggregator site. (We did not use Rotten Tomatoes because the website changed its audience-score methodology in 2019.) Then we matched the reviews with box-office data from The Numbers, a film-industry database.

Talk of a critic-audience divide, it turns out, is overblown. For most of the past 20 years, reviewers and moviegoers have been in broad agreement. Around a decade ago, their views began to diverge. But by 2025 critic and audience ratings were more aligned than at any point since 2005 (see chart 1).

The real difference is not how critics and audiences rate films, but which films they rate. For every ten audience reviews of a documentary, there are six from critics. For dramas and comedies there are around three, and for action less than one. Foreign-language and low-budget films attract disproportionately more attention from critics than from audiences.

Critics and audiences may gravitate towards different films, yet their judgments often align. Between 2005 and 2016 the correlation between critic and audience scores—where zero implies no relationship and one means the scores move perfectly in step—averaged around 0.6. Then opinions began to diverge. Before 2017 a ten-point increase in a film’s audience score was associated with a ten-point increase in its critic score. Over the next six years, that figure fell to just eight points. The correlation between critic and audience scores also dropped from 0.6 to around 0.5. In short, critics’ enthusiasm for a film told you less about how much viewers liked it.

To understand why, we tested a few hypotheses. The first was that the mix of films had changed, as film critics and audiences tend to agree more on some genres than others. But changes in genre, budget, sequel status and studio did little to explain the degree of disagreement.

In fact, much of the divergence happened within two of Hollywood’s biggest categories: big-budget action and family films. Before 2017 critics’ opinions of these films tracked audience opinions about as closely as they did for any other genre. Between 2017 and 2022, however, that relationship collapsed: critics’ scores on such releases were a poor guide to how audiences would rate them. All told, we estimate that roughly 43% of the divergence between critics and audiences was concentrated in these two types of film.

Most industry experts attribute the deviation to franchise fatigue. “Film reviewers got tired of superhero movies before the general audience did,” says Bruce Nash of The Numbers. “It gets boring”, says Mattias Frey of City St George’s, University of London, “if you’re seeing ‘Fast and Furious 23’ or ‘Avengers Part 27’.”

Political polarisation may have also played a part. When studios cast more female and minority actors in big-budget franchises, or embrace “woke” themes—as Marvel Studios did with “Captain Marvel”, its first female-led film, which was described as a “big feminist movie”—audiences tend to be more critical.

Since 2022 critics and audiences have found more common ground. Across all major genres, the correlation between their ratings now sits at nearly 0.7. Some reckon the film industry’s woes may be a factor: reviewers may be going easier on films they would once have panned. “There is this idea that there’s an existential crisis in movies, and that may be changing the way critics operate,” says Daniel Parris, a data scientist. James McMahon, an entertainment researcher, agrees: “As a critic, if you crap on every movie, you may be sinking the very thing that you really love.”

Journalism’s woes may be a factor, too. The era of the esteemed staff reviewer is long over. (“The Last Movie Critic”, a documentary about Roger Ebert, puts it bluntly.) Publications have laid off scores of arts journalists; those who remain must compete with influencers and podcasters to take part in the cultural conversation. They cannot afford to ignore the biggest blockbusters—or write only for the cognoscenti.

All this raises the question of what film critics are for today. Our data suggest they still have commercial clout. We found that higher critic scores are associated with significantly higher ticket sales in America, even after controlling for factors including genre and budget.

Their allure is also intellectual. Critics “get you thinking about things that you might not have thought about”, says Kevin Goetz, an entertainment researcher. Many read reviews only after they have seen a film as a way of extending the experience, positive or negative. Everyone can appreciate a good roast.

articles.title: The latest must-have movie memorabilia? Popcorn buckets
articles.deck: Novelty collectibles are lucrative for cinemas

paragraphs.text: THE NEW “Resident Evil” film depicts a work assignment from hell. Bryan, a medical courier, is asked to deliver a package to a hospital in the mountains; on the way, he has to fight off mutant dogs, rats and people infected with a zombification virus. Fans have been coughing up around $20-25 for the official popcorn bucket, which takes the form of Bryan’s green, bespattered courier bag. (Talk about a bloody good snack.) It has sold out in many cinemas.

Popcorn buckets are popping off. AMC, a cinema chain, has estimated they will bring in $100m in revenue this year, almost double the amount in 2023. “The Odyssey” had buckets shaped like a Trojan horse (for a cool $70) and an imax film camera ($50). “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”, this year’s top-grossing film so far, offered fans the opportunity to dip into a tin shaped like the titular superhero’s head. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” went for a chic red handbag.

These novelty collectibles first went viral in 2024, with the bucket created for “Dune: Part Two”. Inspired by the sandworm that lives on the fictional desert planet of Arrakis, it featured a toothy creature emerging from the dunes. Some, however, felt it resembled a sex toy, and it was lampooned on “Saturday Night Live” and a late-night talk show. (It has become something of a cult item, having listed for $40-800 on resale sites.) Zinc Group, the marketing firm behind the dubious design, did not see the memes coming.

It was the enthusiastic reaction to a “Star Wars” R2-D2 collectible in 2019 that showed how turning a quintessential element of a film into memorabilia can delight fans. “It’s about the tangible experience with the movie that you’re going to see,” says Marcus Gonzalez, global creative director at Zinc. Creative keepsakes help fans feel connected with the film long after the credits roll.

Popcorn buckets are a “status symbol”, argues Calvin Innes, a creative strategist. Well, sort of. Often there is a limited supply, meaning that people who rush to the cinema on a film’s opening weekend are more likely to get their hands on one. Owning a limited-edition item signals to other obsessive fans that you are one of them.

The hype is great news for cinemas, which need to lure customers. Concessions—food and drinks—allow them to squeeze more profit from every moviegoer and popcorn buckets are a way to turn fans’ enthusiasm into high-margin sales. For Vue, a British cinema chain, sales of collectible merchandise have increased ten-fold since 2023.

Design is key. A “well-executed popcorn bucket is a really delightful kind of object” to people of all ages, avers Tim Sparrow, director of retail at Cineworld, another chain: it makes the film experience “so much richer”. The best popcorn buckets turn a movie reference into something playful and nostalgic. They have become such a successful marketing tool that fans are almost as excited to see the popcorn bucket for “Dune: Part Three” as they are to see the film itself in December. Now that’s something for film executives to chew on.

articles.title: How Ella Langley two-stepped to the top of the charts
articles.deck: Country music is riding high, thanks to a new generation of stars and fans

paragraphs.text: THE RECORD for the longest stint atop the Billboard Hot 100, a chart of America’s most popular songs, once belonged to Mariah Carey’s schmaltzy festive anthem, “All I Want For Christmas Is You”. No longer. “Choosin’ Texas”, a twangy country song by Ella Langley, now claims that distinction, having spent 24 weeks in the number-one slot. (Though it was recently bumped to second place by Taylor Swift’s new single.) Ms Langley’s track about being dumped in a honky-tonk may seem like a replay of the genre’s whisky-and-heartbreak trope. In fact, her ascent shows how the country-music business is finding a new rhythm.

Country music has traditionally relied on radio to reach its fans. But it is now America’s fourth-most-streamed genre, after R&B/hip-hop, rock and pop, according to Luminate, an analytics firm. Spotify reports that global streams passed 90bn last year and royalties have grown more than 130% since 2020. More labels are setting up shop in Nashville and Austin. Pop stars have climbed the charts after donning cowboy boots. This year Ms Swift, who started out as a country singer before turning to pop, returned to the genre with the single “I Knew It, I Knew You”. (There are rumours that her next album will offer more boot-scootin’ tunes.)

Ms Langley is currently touring her second album across America. Her monthly listeners on Spotify, the biggest streamer, have soared by 20m in a year. Her breakout success combines old-world pastoral charm with an astute use of social media.

She grew up in Hope Hull, Alabama, where the population is just over 7,000. (Her first audience, she has joked, was a bunch of cows.) She hunts and claims to have learned to read by singing hymns at church. In 2019, aged 20, Ms Langley moved to Nashville to become a songwriter. She signed a record deal in 2023 after performing at the Grand Ole Opry, a hallowed venue in the city that made stars of Loretta Lynn and Dolly Parton.

Yet Ms Langley has made her name on social-media platforms as well as Nashville’s stages. She posted a clip of herself singing in her car in 2021, which went viral; a publishing deal followed soon after. Her internet fame resulted in collaborations with more established stars. In 2024 a snippet of a single from her debut album, “Hungover”, again went viral on TikTok.

Gen Z is charmed by the aesthetics of Americana. So the arrival of digitally native stars like Ms Langley, now 27, came at a “perfect moment”, says Jaime Marconette of Luminate. The firm has found that country-music fans are 27% more likely than the average American to use TikTok, giving performers more opportunities to be discovered. They are also more likely to listen on repeat to their favourite songs and artists, which keeps the music in the charts. The mellow strains of “Choosin’ Texas” have no doubt worked in its favour: it can be listened to again and again without its hooks becoming grating.

People who listen to music on streaming platforms tend not to seek out a specific genre, but a playlist that suits a mood or activity, such as cooking, explains Emily Cohen Belote of Amazon Music. This can help songs reach unexpected audiences. The guitar riffs of “Choosin’ Texas” may appeal to fans of 1980s soft rock. Ms Langley’s husky voice recalls Sheryl Crow.

Still, the number of people choosing “Choosin’ Texas” is surprising. A country track usually has to blend with another genre to “have this massive pop crossover moment”, says Claire Heinichen of Spotify. That is not the case with Ms Langley’s hit, which declares: “A cowboy always finds a way to leave / Drinkin’ Jack all by myself.” The appeal is in the storytelling. The lyrics might portray a “very specific Southern experience”, admits Ms Heinichen. “But being sad in a bar is universal.”

articles.title: Leadership lessons from Napoleon
articles.deck: How the French emperor’s management style ultimately led to his fall

paragraphs.text: What management tips can you learn from conquerors? Put aside oppression, and there are lessons about delegation, motivation, recruitment and team building. Alexander the Great refused to drink water before battle to stand in solidarity with his men. Caesar marched on foot alongside his men, even swimming across rivers, to demonstrate his derring-do. When his army wobbled, he would fling himself in the way of his fleeing men, “even catching them by the throat and forcing them to face the enemy”, according to Suetonius, a Roman historian. Diocletian divided the Roman Empire into four, and shared power while keeping a firm central grip.

In 2014 Andrew Roberts, a prolific British historian and member of the House of Lords, published an excellent biography of Napoleon and his boldness on the battlefield. In a new book he examines Napoleon’s marshal system. The day after he proclaimed himself emperor of France in 1804, Napoleon appointed 18 “marshals of the empire”, later increasing the tally to 26. They were to be “the swords around Napoleon’s throne”, the army’s most venerated figures and the pinnacle of French society.

Some recruits came from the nobility; others were craftsmen’s sons. They were indulged with fortunes, land and even marriages into the imperial family. Each was given a deep-blue velvet high-collared uniform trimmed with golden embroidery, complete with a red silk sash, and a baton inscribed with the gold imperial eagles. Napoleon made six of them princes and crowned two kings.

The marshals’ elite leadership team was built to carry out Napoleon’s orders and bring glory to France by executing his new theory of warfare, with fewer set-piece sieges and more agile manoeuvres, thanks to an army that lived off the land. But Napoleon also devised an efficient modern management system, based on the recruitment of brilliant talent, doling out of lavish rewards, intolerance of weakness and a demand for total loyalty.

For all this Napoleon relied heavily on Louis-Alexandre Berthier, his chief of staff, first marshal and a skilled manager with a remarkable grasp of detail. A short, strong man who was said to be able to fall asleep with one eye open, Berthier was a former topographical engineer who had volunteered to sail across the Atlantic to help the Americans in their war for independence, drawing up a detailed map of the coast of Rhode Island.

Berthier divided the army staff into four branches, to cover everything from intelligence to supplies. Divisional commanders had to provide twice-daily updates on the whereabouts of every soldier; these dossiers, like proto-spreadsheets, were sent in 18 large volumes twice a month from the war ministry to Napoleon. In Berthier’s written orders “all names of places, rivers, enemy generals and regiments were underlined,” writes Lord Roberts. New information flowed constantly, from gunpowder stocks or the provision of shoes to the state of troops’ morale. Berthier and Napoleon travelled in a coach fitted with cupboards and drawers for books, maps and a card index listing the location of every unit of the Grande Armée.

To motivate his marshals, Napoleon issued performance reviews in campaign bulletins, showering praise for heroic achievements along with crushing criticism. Success was rewarded. An attentive manager, Napoleon also liked to offer his marshals personalised advice on how to galvanise the troops. “Do not neglect to fanaticise the soldier and to electrify his imagination to the utmost,” he wrote to André Masséna as he was facing the Austrian army.

Yet in the end the management system failed him. As the empire expanded, Napoleon insisted on total control, cramped his marshals’ autonomy and undermined their effectiveness. Worse, he came to weaken the very system he had built. His incentive scheme became capricious, as he overlooked those who deserved praise in some campaign bulletins, or used marshals as scapegoats.

Rather than generating creative tension, he fostered destructive rivalry. The danger, Lord Roberts notes, was “when marshals started to see warfare not as a team enterprise so much as a race among rivals for individual triumph and fame”. Napoleon even boasted of stoking “continual jealousy”: “I am careful to keep my ministers and generals at variance among themselves, in order that each may reveal to me the faults of the other.”

The marshals began to come to blows after Napoleon’s victory over the combined Russian and Austrian armies at Austerlitz in 1805, and things just got worse. For all his skill, writes Lord Roberts, “Napoleon had a great capacity for sheer spitefulness.” By the time the emperor rode into his last battle in 1815, only two marshals accompanied him. Napoleon’s “approach to leadership”, the author notes, “ultimately left him almost completely bereft of the support he so desperately needed as he faced his Waterloo”.

articles.title: How personal rivalries and clashes are shaping the AI race
articles.deck: A new book offers a rollicking tale of the people shaping Silicon Valley’s new obsession

paragraphs.text: To someone who has not witnessed the AI scene in California’s Bay Area, it is hard to convey how utterly weird it is. The Curve, a recent conference, hosted sessions including “What’s the plan for keeping robots under control?” and “The Neural Frontier: what happens when AI can read your mind?” People lounged on couches and in gazebos with cold brews and kombuchas discussing how AI company staff made obscenely rich by forthcoming public offerings should channel their philanthropic giving—even as some of them conspired to hobble their own employers to delay civilisational upheaval.

The goal of Kevin Roose, a former reporter for the New York Times, was not to write a grand treatise on what AI means for the world but merely to record this weirdness before it was lost to the vagaries of memory, disappearing message threads and obsolete media-storage formats. In “The AGI Chronicles” his focus is the nine years since Google researchers developed the transformer, the type of AI model that underlies ChatGPT and all its kin. Quickly the idea took hold that, given enough data and computing power, transformer-based systems would eventually attain the holy grail: a truly “general” AI, or AGI, matching human smarts and then outstripping them.

That doctrine has been the driving force of AI research ever since. And so its history in the West mostly boils down to the interwoven fates of a handful of brilliant, prickly people raising ever more money, panicking each time they get leapfrogged by rivals and splitting off in a blaze of acrimony to start their own firms.

In outline, much of the story will be familiar. But Mr Roose captures the madness in a fast-paced style. His account is filled with gossipy anecdotes that highlight just how much the ambitions, ideological divides and personality clashes of a group small enough to fit in a couple of classrooms have shaped what may turn out to be the most consequential technology in modern history. As Mr Roose puts it, AGI is a “quest that half my sources thought was going to save the world, and the other half thought was going to end it”.

Consider Dario Amodei, who early in his tenure at OpenAI proposed the doctrine that more data and more compute equals more intelligence. He eventually left to form Anthropic, in part because he thought OpenAI was reneging on its original commitment to build AI safely, and in part because he considered Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, “a bully, a credit hog, and a cut-throat capitalist”, in Mr Roose’s words. Mr Brockman, in turn, thought Mr Amodei was a “paranoid control freak who used safety as a pretext to win arguments”.

For years, AGI was seen as the prize in an all-or-nothing contest to whose winner all power in the world would accrue. But as the goal approached, definitions multiplied to the point where the term has lost all meaning. At some point in 2025, Mr Roose noticed a shift in rhetoric. There would never be a finish line, only an endless arms race. By then, some researchers were starting to be terrified by their creations’ power—but “they kept accelerating, because they had forgotten how to do anything else.”

Meanwhile, Mr Roose provocatively argues that AGI has, in fact, quietly arrived. A few dollars now buys you some time with an intelligence that is tolerably good at a growing number of things and extraordinary at a few; not human-level (yet), but already pretty general.

Perhaps that is why hardly anybody mentioned “AGI” at The Curve. The talk was of “extremely powerful AI” and “advanced superintelligence”. The names and goalposts change, the relentless pursuit of computing capability continues, and with it the efforts of a small group of people, alternately elated and horrified at the creation taking shape before them.

articles.title: Are there too many art fairs?
articles.deck: Probably. But FOMO keeps collectors and dealers going to them

paragraphs.text: ART COLLECTORS are like swallows. They flock together, preen and feed (on canapés and champagne). They also migrate seasonally. In October they roost in Paris during Art Basel, which runs from October 21st-25th. (The early birds landed in London for Frieze, another art fair, the previous week.) In December they head to Miami; in March to Maastricht; in May to New York; and in June to the original Basel in Switzerland. And that does not include the more adventurous ones, who zoom off to fairs in Doha, Hong Kong and Seoul.

It is as exhausting as it sounds. “Everyone is talking about art-fair fatigue,” says Aurelie Cauchy of the Twentieth, an advisory firm. In 2025 there were 370 major art fairs—more than one for every day of the year. That is up from around 55 in 2000, says Clare McAndrew, an art economist. Can collectors and dealers maintain their current pace? Beneath the glass roof of the sun-drenched Grand Palais, where Art Basel Paris takes place, there is more gloom than the Instagram posts would have you believe (and not just because of the recent unrest in France).

Gallerists are facing what the French call a choix cornélien (difficult choice), says Ms Cauchy. The cost of keeping a physical storefront is growing, but fewer clients are casually popping in. Recently, some have had to lay off staff or close up entirely. Dealers feel pressure to keep travelling to fairs in order to find new clients and keep the artists they represent happy.

But this carries an ever-growing price tag, which many struggle to afford. Shipping costs are triple what they were before covid-19, says Thaddaeus Ropac, a prominent gallerist. (It’s not just getting there; all unsold works have to be shipped back.) Gallerists’ own travel costs have travelled higher, too. And the booths themselves have become more expensive to rent and build. Art Basel, for example, charges around $29,000 for its smallest booth and more than $177,000 for the largest. (The square-metre price for large exhibitors is 32% more in real terms than in 2018.) Those fees just get you floor space: exhibitors need to rent carpet, lighting and add other design features. “Fairs are becoming a burden,” especially for smaller and mid-sized galleries, says Valentina Castellani, an art-market expert.
Costs have changed the art that appears in fairs. Sculptures are so expensive to ship that they rarely make financial sense. Nor do items with lower price tags, such as many photographs.

Since fairs first arrived on the art scene in the 1960s-70s, collectors have found them worthwhile because of their scale and efficiency (so much art is packed into a small space). But art enthusiasts now have fair complaints. One is crowds. Fairs have a lot of guests and such long queues that you’d be forgiven for thinking VIP stands for “very immobile people”. Basel has responded by launching a VVIP preview, Avant-Première, an evening before the VIP opening to offer buyers more quietude. Meanwhile, collectors are culling their calendars and choosing to attend fewer fairs. This month some Americans put the freeze on Frieze and opted to attend only Art Basel Paris instead.

In the future there may be fewer international fairs. People do not want to see the same gallerists everywhere. To lure collectors, organisers will need to offer a more distinctive experience, with more local galleries and artists. This is a broader trend beyond art. “We’ve gone from a moment where everything was meta-globalist to regionalisation,” says Noah Horowitz, the boss of Art Basel. Some gallerists are excited, thinking they may participate in fewer fairs but encounter new local collectors at the ones they do. In art and in commerce, sometimes less is more.

articles.title: Economic data, commodities and markets
Jeffrey Archer’s career was worthy of his most improbable plots
articles.deck: The bestselling novelist, conman and politician died on October 5th, aged 86

paragraphs.text: “Could it work?” Archer asked himself. “Why on earth not?” his alter ego replied.

He stood in the penthouse living room where, for years, dinners of shepherd’s pie and Krug had been served up to London’s finest. From the floor-to-ceiling windows he stared down at the Shard, the Eye, the Cheese Grater and the Palace of Westminster, all embraced by the gleaming River Thames. Behind him, in the vast lounge, a Picasso and a Monet adorned the walls.

Settling into the overstuffed cream sofa, he felt almost insanely satisfied with his life. Yes, it would be well worth writing up. Rags-to-riches stories were his stock-in-trade, and the riches had come from his own efforts. More than 330m of his 31 page-turner novels had been sold in 114 countries. (The Monet was a bonus from his third, “Kane and Abel”.) There had been seven sets of short stories, three plays and even a Gospel. Not long ago, in India, a beggar boy at a traffic light had tried to sell him “the latest Jeffrey Archer”. “I am the latest Jeffrey Archer!” he had joyfully cried.

Besides all that he had climbed to the heights of British politics, sprinting there as he’d done to set an Oxford record in 1966: 100 yards in under ten seconds, earning him an Athletics Blue. Up and up, from Tory councillor for Havering to MP for Louth in Lincolnshire, to deputy chairman of the Conservative Party, to the House of Lords as Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, his childhood home. He served humble fare at his parties to remind himself and his influential guests how far and fast he had come.
Yet it could have been even faster and farther, if not for certain trip-ups on the way.

The summer sun beat down with unusual heat on the lawns of the Old Vicarage at Grantchester, former residence of the poet Rupert Brooke. There was honey, his own, for tea. Archer was in the thatched summerhouse, within earshot of a tinkling antique fountain, trying to write. Staedtler pencils and lined A4 paper were ranged in front of him.

However, words were not flowing. He very rarely suffered from writer’s block, but this side of his career was painful. It had ended in the hell of Belmarsh, a category A prison where, after exchanging his Hilditch & Key shirt, his Aquascutum jacket and his House of Commons cufflinks for prison garb, he was conducted to a filthy cell with a hard mattress and an open lavatory with no flush.

Yet distinction had been his keynote. He implied he had been to Wellington, the public school, rather than Wellington School in Somerset. He had left with 3 O-levels, but slid into a Dip Ed at Oxford and emerged, after three sporting years, as an alumnus of Brasenose. Then he had set up a fake body-building course.

Like father, like son. After indulging in mortgage frauds Archer père had fled the country, ending up as a chewing-gum salesman in New York. Archer fils followed by fiddling his expenses in one short-lived job and then, in 1974, almost bankrupting himself by buying 105,000 shares in a fraudulent scheme. He lost almost £500,000; writing rescued him. He had just enough cash to stay on as an MP, but did not stand for re-election. Only two things saved his political skin. One was his charity work, though at times it raised less than he claimed. The second was the support of Margaret Thatcher and John Major who propelled him, despite his leftward lean, up the party ladder away from the snakes beneath.
But then came a particularly unfortunate encounter.

On the terrace of his villa in Mallorca, once the property of Yves St Laurent, Archer pondered. Before him stretched a favourite view, the Bay of Palma and the rugged Mediterranean coast. His wife of many years, Mary, once accurately described as “fragrant”, had brought him a cup of coffee and a plate of assorted biscuits. To steel himself, he took a chocolate one.

He had always been a charmer. Mrs T. had visibly kindled in his presence, and there were not a few affairs. However, in 1986 he insisted that pure philanthropy led him to pay £2,000 to a prostitute, Monica Coghlan, to persuade her to go abroad. The story led in the News of the World and, with more sex, the Daily Star. He sued, and won damages of £500,000. But the Star kept on his case, and in 2001 Archer went down for four years for perjury and obstruction of justice, besides losing the damages. The Tory Party expelled him for five years and the MCC suspended him for seven.
He could never fathom what perjury had to do with cricket.

Evening had arrived, and his A4 was still blank. Perhaps this really was too tall a tale, even for a master storyteller. For, after all that, he was still rich. His charity work was still admired, and prison had softened him. He even remained a member of the House of Lords. And people would undoubtedly go on reading him.

Fine literature was not his element, but he liked Puck. His version of him, performed at college in his 20s, had been a wicked elf, kicking people, leaping hedges and endlessly provoking Shakespeare’s midsummer lovers. Yet Puck was also kindly Robin Goodfellow. It was as both that on October 4th at London's Leicester Square Theatre he bade farewell to his public: eager fans, rude critics, jealous writers, offended politicians. The whole lot.

articles.title: Politics

paragraphs.text: Donald Trump rejected a deal offered by Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial vessels within seven days and resume nuclear talks if America lifts its blockade of Iranian ports. He told aides he expected to begin bombing Iran again after the midterm elections in November. Mr Trump said America had “total control” of the strait and that “massive amounts of oil” were passing through it.

The last American and British troops left Iraq, ending their presence in the country since 2014, when they were sent as part of an international coalition to fight Islamic State, a jihadist group. The Iraqi prime minister said their departure heralded a shift to Iraq taking “full responsibility for its security and stability”.

A Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia when it plunged nearly 20,000 feet in less than two minutes and issued a distress signal, after a co-pilot stabbed the captain. Israel Katz, the Israeli defence minister, claimed that early evidence suggested the rogue pilot had intended to crash the plane, killing everyone on board, and called it an “attempted jihadist terror attack”. Passengers tackled the attacker, allowing other pilots to land the plane. Binyamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, described the Indian captain as a “true hero” for fighting back.

Fatima Zahra El Mansouri was appointed Morocco’s first female prime minister, after her liberal party won the most seats in a recent parliamentary election. King Mohammed VI chose Ms Mansouri, a former mayor of Marrakesh, over Fouzi Lekjaa, her party colleague and head of the football federation.

Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, and William Ruto, Kenya’s president, broke ground on a $16bn refinery in Lamu on Kenya’s coast, which they hope will reduce fuel costs and import bills for refined products in east Africa. Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopia’s prime minister, Yoweri Museveni, Uganda’s president, and several other African leaders attended the ceremony. Mr Dangote already operates a big refinery in his native Nigeria.

Umaro Sissoco Embaló, the former president of Guinea-Bissau, who was ousted in a coup in November 2025, said he would return to the country to stand in presidential elections on December 6th. The announcement added fuel to suspicions that Mr Embaló orchestrated the coup, which happened just before the publication of results in an election he had been expected to lose.

The summit between Mr Trump and Xi Jinping produced no big breakthroughs, though China and America did agree to reduce tariffs on $30bn-worth of each other’s goods, not including soyabeans, and said they would set up a US-China Super-Intelligence Dialogue (China calls it an AI dialogue). This would include a mechanism for reporting AI incidents.

Britain’s MI5 intelligence service warned British academics that the China General Technology Research Institute in Beijing had strong ties to Chinese intelligence, and was funding research to aid China’s espionage operations. MI5 said academics were probably unaware of the links, but urged universities to cut their ties with the CGTRI, and said they could be in violation of national-security laws if they did not.

Malaysia began repatriating the first batch of 5,000 asylum-seekers to Myanmar under a plan that it has co-ordinated with the Burmese junta. Refugees from Myanmar’s Rohingya Muslim population have encountered a wave of hostility in Malaysia, facing forced evictions from villages and schools. There are thought to be 126,000 Rohingya in the country. The government insists the repatriations are voluntary, but UN personnel have been barred from screening them. It is unclear if any Rohingya were in the first batch of refugees to leave.

In Myanmar at least 50 people were reportedly killed by an air strike in the town of Kyauktaw, close to the border with Bangladesh. The strike was the latest offensive by Myanmar’s armed forces against the Arakan Army, a separatist group that has also committed atrocities against the Rohingya.

The death toll from flooding in Thailand rose to 23. Bangkok was inundated with 32cm (12.6 inches) of rain over three days, hampering operations at its main airport. The waters started to recede in the centre of the city, but outlying suburbs were expected to take longer to drain. More heavy rain is forecast for the capital soon.

Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv was hit by a drone in another Russian barrage across the capital. At least two people were killed at the academy, which was formed in 1918 and co-ordinates research at Ukraine’s leading institutes.

Counter-terrorism police in Britain said that no explosive devices had been found in a van used by five men initially suspected of attempting to attack Fairford air base, where American bombers take off on sorties attacking military installations in Iran. The British government held an emergency COBRA security meeting after the five men were arrested, but, despite official suspicions of Iranian involvement, they were released on bail pending further investigation.

Andy Burnham, who took over as Britain’s prime minister in July, gave his big speech to the Labour Party conference in Liverpool. Enjoying a bounce in the polls, Mr Burnham delivered a message of “hope again” and said he wanted to draw a line under a decade of division. He pledged to tackle three thorny issues: state pensions, the voting system and Europe, though those reforms were pushed back to after the next general election, which is not due until 2029 (Mr Burnham did announce a national commission to study electoral reform). Labour’s opponents said his speech did nothing to tackle the problems Britain faces today.

In France Edouard Philippe, the leading centre-right candidate for president in next year’s election, outlined a pension-reform plan that would raise the minimum retirement age from nearly 63 to 65. Mr Philippe described the country’s comparatively low age of retirement as unsustainable, saying that without reform there was a risk of a financial crisis. New statistics showed that public debt has risen again, to 119% of GDP. France’s sovereign borrowing costs rose to their highest level since 2008. The government unveiled its budget for 2027, promising €54bn ($61bn) in savings. But it says the deficit will be 5% of GDP, well above the EU’s 3% cap.

The first woman to face execution in Tennessee for 200 years survived the procedure to kill her by lethal injection. Christa Pike was convicted in 1996 for murdering a classmate when she was 18. She was transferred to a medical facility after the botched execution. The prisons authority insisted that the proper protocols were followed and that she had been injected with two syringes of lethal-injection chemicals.

The candidates in Brazil’s presidential contest entered the final stage of campaigning before the election on October 4th. The left-wing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, holds a slim lead over his conservative challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, but that narrows to a statistical tie in the expected run-off election on October 25th.

Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, ranted on social media about the Falkland Islands, and threatened to take legal action against an Anglo-Israeli oil-exploration project in the area within two weeks unless it ceases operations. Mr Milei has described the project as a “clear and present danger” to Argentina. He recently rounded on the UN for not moving forward on Argentina’s claims of sovereignty over the British territory, describing the UN as “useless” and stuffed with “arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”.

articles.title: Business

paragraphs.text: Details emerged about Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, which it has circulated among key investors. According to Reuters, revenue at the firm reportedly rose to $4.6bn last year, and it recorded a net loss of $42bn, $34bn of which was an accounting charge. It aims to spend $518bn in the near future on cloud infrastructure and other investments. Anthropic could be valued at $2trn when it lists on the stock market, which would smash the record $1.8trn valuation set by SpaceX only in June. The IPO is not expected until after America’s midterm elections in November. It counted “existential risks to humanity” among the hazards facing its business.

Sam Altman, the boss of OpenAI, said his firm’s already-delayed IPO would not take place until it had tackled concerns about the safety of its technology. OpenAI confirmed that it had withheld the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after its new model displayed high levels of deception during internal tests. It also suspended trials of other models. The firm has admitted that its agents breached dozens of systems, including some governmental ones.

Confronting worries about AI safety, Nvidia launched an Open Agent Safety Platform that allows companies to track the activities of their AI agents. Jensen Huang, the chipmaker’s boss, is less concerned about the threat from AI to humanity than his fellow tech titans, saying recently that it is up to AI companies to ensure their models are safe and under control. Meanwhile, Nvidia expanded its share buy-back programme by $150bn, taking its total buy-back plan to $235bn, the biggest-ever in corporate America.

AMD struck an agreement to acquire World Labs, a startup, in an $8.2bn deal. World Labs was co-founded by Fei-Fei Li, a leading AI researcher and professor at Stanford University, to develop spatial models that investigate how the three-dimensional physical world works for application in areas such as robotics and gaming. AMD’s acquisition is the latest instance of a chipmaker evolving its business towards the development of advanced AI frontier models.

The sell-off in bond markets continued. The yield on ten-year US Treasuries was over 5.3%, its highest level since 2002. British 30-year gilts crossed 6% and French spreads over German Bunds were back to euro-crisis levels. Donald Trump didn’t help by renewing his call for Jerome Powell to step down from the board of governors at the Federal Reserve, which revived fears about the independence of the central bank and the direction of inflation.

Shein’s first earnings report since listing on the stock market in early September disappointed investors. Adjusted net profit fell by 67%, year on year, and revenue was virtually flat. The ultra-cheap retailer’s share price plunged after it announced its results, giving it a market value of around $17bn, down from $26bn at its IPO.

The German government was reportedly seeking assurances from UniCredit, an Italian bank, about its commitments in any takeover of Commerzbank, Germany’s second-biggest lender, such as keeping its listing in Frankfurt. The government has so far resisted UniCredit’s advances on Commerzbank, but has moderated its opposition to a deal. The Italians are preparing to take control as early as January next year, according to reports, and plan a big restructuring of the bank, including ditching some international business.

Tata Trusts, the charitable group which owns 66% of Tata Sons, proposed merging the holding company with two subsidiaries to avoid a forced public listing. The proposal, led by Noel Tata, a scion of the Tata family, challenges the board’s recent decision to proceed with an IPO.

SpaceX’s Starship rocket marked a milestone by reaching orbit for the first time, despite a failure in one of its three main engines, which cut short its flying time. The mission deployed 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, which increase capacity and data density for Starlink’s broadband service.

Walmart promised its customers that it would not use AI to “set different prices based on who you are or the time of day”. The supermarket chain was responding to concerns about the prospect of retailers using AI to determine a price based on a shopper’s individual data. The Federal Trade Commission has warned recently that businesses that don’t tell consumers their data is being used this way may be breaking the law. Dynamic pricing has long been in use, but now McDonald’s and other fast-food chains are reportedly experimenting with sophisticated algorithms to decide prices based on local demand, so a Big Mac could cost more in one outlet than another nearby.

Authoritarians have a secret Achilles heel: City Hall
